title: Wall Street Rebounds as Oil Retreats and CPI Lands in Line
content: US stocks rallied on Friday, snapping a four-day losing streak, as retreating oil prices and an in-line inflation report calmed nerves after a turbulent week dominated by the Middle East conflict. The S&P 500 climbed 0.9% and both the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the Nasdaq Composite added 1.0%, though all three indices still finished the week lower as the energy-driven surge in Treasury yields weighed on sentiment.
summary: US equities bounced on Friday as oil eased and August CPI matched forecasts, but Wall Street still closed a choppy week in the red.
context:
• Markets spent the week whipsawed by an oil shock triggered by the Iran war, which drove crude above $100 a barrel and pushed Treasury yields to multi-year highs.

• Investors had been positioned for steady Fed policy, but the energy-led inflation scare revived speculation the central bank could turn more hawkish at its 15-16 September meeting.

• Technology megacaps had led a summer rally, leaving richly valued indices sensitive to any renewed climb in the discount rate.
happened:
• The S&P 500 rose 0.9% to snap a four-session slide, while the Dow and the Nasdaq each gained 1.0%.

• August CPI rose 0.4% month on month and 3.4% year on year, matching consensus and easing fears sparked by the prior day's hot producer-price data.

• Crude retreated — WTI fell 2.4% to settle at $100.05 and Brent slid 2.8% to $104.61 — while the 2-year Treasury yield topped 4.6%, its highest since July 2024; for the week the Dow lost 1.6% and the S&P 500 fell 0.8%.
implications:
• With the FOMC due to meet on 15-16 September, any further spike in oil or inflation expectations could tilt the Fed towards holding firm or even tightening, a hawkish risk for equities.

• High-multiple technology names remain the most exposed if the front end of the curve keeps repricing higher.

• A durable de-escalation in the Middle East is now the clearest catalyst for a broader risk-on move.
importance:
• The week showed how quickly a geopolitical energy shock can override an otherwise benign US macro backdrop.

• Friday's bounce signals dip-buying appetite persists, but narrow leadership leaves indices vulnerable to headline risk.

• The inflation-yields-equity linkage is back at the centre of the market, raising the stakes on every data point and Fed signal.

title: Asian Markets Slide as Oil Surge and Bond Rout Bite
content: Asian equities fell broadly on Friday, tracking the global bond sell-off and the spike in oil prices as the Middle East conflict escalated. Japan's Nikkei 225 tumbled 1.93% to 64,011.34, weighed further by expectations of a Bank of Japan rate rise, while mainland China's Shanghai Composite dropped 1.18% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng eased 0.60%.
summary: Asian markets sold off on Friday as surging oil and rising global yields hit risk appetite across the region.
context:
• The regional retreat followed a sharp jump in crude and a global bond rout sparked by intensifying US-Iran hostilities around the Strait of Hormuz.

• Japanese equities faced an added headwind from mounting bets on a Bank of Japan hike at its 17-18 September meeting.

• Higher energy import costs are a particular drag for oil-dependent Asian economies, threatening corporate margins and current-account balances.
happened:
• The Nikkei 225 fell 1.93% to 64,011.34 and the TOPIX slipped 0.65% to 4,028.30.

• The Shanghai Composite declined 1.18% to 3,888.11, while the Hang Seng lost 0.60% to 24,805.63.

• The moves mirrored Wall Street's mid-week slide and the surge in global government bond yields.
implications:
• A stronger yen on BOJ tightening would pressure Japanese exporters even as it eases imported-energy costs.

• Sustained high oil prices could widen trade deficits across import-reliant economies such as India, Japan and South Korea.

• Chinese equities remain caught between external energy pressure and hopes for further domestic stimulus.
importance:
• Asia's open often sets the tone for global risk sentiment, and Friday's declines underscored the worldwide reach of the oil shock.

• The BOJ decision is a pivotal near-term catalyst for regional currencies and rates.

• Energy-driven inflation complicates the easing paths several Asian central banks had been contemplating.

title: Yen Firms Near Seven-Month High Ahead of BOJ Decision
content: The Japanese yen held near a seven-month high against the dollar, trading around 153 per dollar, as traders positioned for a Bank of Japan rate rise at its 17-18 September meeting. The currency has gained more than 3% this month, supported by hawkish BOJ expectations, the unwinding of carry trades and repatriation flows, even as a global bond sell-off lifted yields elsewhere.
summary: The yen firmed towards a seven-month high as markets priced in a likely Bank of Japan rate rise next week.
context:
• The BOJ lifted its policy rate to 1% in June, the highest since 1995, and board hawk Hajime Takata has pushed for a move to 1.25%.

• Governor Kazuo Ueda has signalled a hike is likely this month, with traders assigning roughly 80% odds to action on 18 September.

• Rising crude prices and persistent above-target inflation have strengthened the case for further Japanese tightening.
happened:
• The yen traded around 153 per dollar, close to its strongest level in seven months, and is up more than 3% in September.

• The BOJ meets on 17-18 September, with markets pricing a strong chance of a rise from the current 1% policy rate.

• Bank of America has forecast the yen could strengthen a further 6% by the end of 2026.
implications:
• A BOJ hike would narrow rate differentials with a still-elevated Fed, a dynamic that favours further yen appreciation.

• Continued yen strength threatens the profits of Japan's large exporters but relieves the cost of dollar-priced energy imports.

• An accelerated unwinding of yen carry trades could ripple through global risk assets, as seen in past episodes.
importance:
• USD/JPY is a key barometer of global risk appetite and funding conditions.

• The BOJ's normalisation marks a historic shift after decades of ultra-loose policy, with cross-border spillovers.

• Currency swings of this scale reshape hedging costs and returns for global investors in Japanese assets.

title: Gold Holds Near Record as War and Inflation Fears Persist
content: Gold held near record highs, trading around $4,350 an ounce, as investors sought safety amid the Iran war and an energy-driven inflation scare. Bullion's advance has been tempered by surging real yields, which raise the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset, leaving prices roughly flat over the past month but still up around 19% on the year.
summary: Gold traded near record levels around $4,350 an ounce as war and inflation fears fuelled haven demand.
context:
• Bullion has set successive record highs through 2026 on geopolitical risk, central-bank buying and inflation hedging.

• The Middle East conflict and the spike in oil prices have reinforced gold's appeal as a store of value.

• However, the sharp rise in Treasury yields has capped gains by lifting the real cost of holding the metal.
happened:
• Spot gold rose 0.76% to about $4,350 an ounce on Friday, near its all-time high.

• December futures had opened the month around $4,522 an ounce, underscoring the metal's elevated levels.

• Over the past month gold is little changed as haven demand and rising yields offset one another, but it remains roughly 19% higher year on year.
implications:
• A further escalation in the Middle East or a renewed inflation surprise could push gold to fresh records.

• Conversely, a sustained climb in real yields or a swift de-escalation would weigh on prices.

• Continued central-bank accumulation provides a structural floor beneath the market.
importance:
• Gold's resilience signals persistent demand for hedges against geopolitical and inflation risk.

• The metal's performance relative to real yields is a closely watched gauge of market stress.

• Record prices affect miners, jewellery demand and the balance sheets of gold-holding central banks.

title: Bitcoin Drops Below $77,000 as Yields and Oil Weigh
content: Bitcoin slid below $77,000 on Friday, extending a week of losses driven by rising Treasury yields, higher oil prices and mounting expectations of tighter monetary policy rather than any crypto-specific catalyst. The token fell about 1.5% to roughly $77,300 after settling near $76,600 on Thursday in the wake of a hotter-than-expected US producer-price report, while Ether slipped to around $2,466.
summary: Bitcoin dropped below $77,000 as surging yields and rate-hike bets pressured risk assets across the board.
context:
• Cryptocurrencies pay no yield, making them sensitive to rising real interest rates that boost the appeal of bonds and cash.

• The week's oil shock and bond sell-off pushed long-dated Treasury yields to multi-decade highs, a broad headwind for speculative assets.

• Bitcoin had already been trading lower on the year despite strong exchange-traded-fund inflows earlier in 2026.
happened:
• Bitcoin fell about 1.5% to around $77,300, having settled near $76,568 on Thursday after the hot PPI print.

• Ether eased about 0.6% to roughly $2,466, tracking bitcoin lower.

• Traders reported around $562m in bitcoin leveraged-position liquidations, including some $484m in long positions.
implications:
• With CME FedWatch showing rising odds of a Fed move next week, further yield increases could keep pressure on crypto.

• A de-escalation in the Middle East or softer inflation data would ease the macro headwinds weighing on digital assets.

• Heavy long liquidations suggest leverage remains a source of near-term volatility.
importance:
• Bitcoin is increasingly trading as a macro risk asset, closely tied to rates and liquidity conditions.

• The sell-off highlights crypto's vulnerability when real yields rise sharply.

• Leverage-driven swings underscore the asset class's sensitivity to shifts in sentiment.

title: Brent Spikes to $108 as US-Iran Conflict Threatens Supply
content: Oil prices soared on Thursday, with Brent crude jumping as much as 7.1% to hit $108 a barrel — its highest since May — as intensifying hostilities between the US and Iran threatened supply routes through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Brent settled 6.34% higher at $107.63 and US crude climbed 6.69% to $102.48 in its biggest one-day jump in six weeks, sending shockwaves through global bonds and equities.
summary: Brent crude spiked to $108 a barrel as US-Iran hostilities threatened key shipping routes, rattling global markets.
context:
• The Middle East conflict has escalated sharply, with the US and Iran trading strikes and Iran-backed Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia and shipping in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

• Saudi Arabia shut its East-West crude pipeline as a precaution, tightening available supply.

• The surge came despite the International Energy Agency cutting its 2026 demand forecast, its largest projected annual decline since the pandemic.
happened:
• Brent rose as much as 7.1% to $108 before settling 6.34% higher at $107.63, its highest close since 19 May.

• US WTI crude hit $103 for the first time since May, settling 6.69% higher at $102.48.

• The oil spike drove the 10-year Treasury yield above 4.97% and pushed global equities lower.
implications:
• Sustained crude above $100 would feed directly into headline inflation, complicating central-bank policy worldwide.

• Any disruption to Strait of Hormuz traffic — a chokepoint for roughly a fifth of global oil — risks a far sharper spike.

• Energy-intensive sectors and import-dependent economies face margin and current-account pressure.
importance:
• Oil is the key transmission channel turning a regional conflict into a global macro shock.

• The move revived the inflation-and-rates fears that had eased over the summer.

• Traders across every asset class are now hostage to Middle East headlines.

title: Treasury Yields Hit Multi-Year Highs Before Buyback Relief
content: Government bonds sold off sharply on Thursday as the oil-driven inflation scare and a hotter-than-expected US producer-price report drove yields to multi-year highs. The 10-year Treasury yield surged more than 10 basis points to 4.97%, its highest since October 2023, while the 30-year topped 5.3%, a level last seen in 2007, prompting the US Treasury to announce it would at least double its long-dated debt buybacks.
summary: Treasury yields spiked to multi-year highs on the oil-inflation shock before easing after the Treasury doubled debt buybacks.
context:
• Bond markets had already been under pressure from persistent inflation and concerns over rising government borrowing.

• The jump in crude prices and a hot PPI print reignited fears the Fed could keep policy tight or even raise rates.

• The sell-off was global, with yields climbing across Europe and Asia.
happened:
• The 10-year yield rose above 4.97% and the 2-year climbed towards 4.54%, while the 30-year exceeded 5.3%.

• The US Treasury said it would lift the maximum size of its buybacks of long-term debt from $2bn to at least $4bn.

• Following the announcement, yields pared gains, with the 30-year falling as much as 9 basis points to 5.19%.
implications:
• Higher long-end yields raise borrowing costs across the economy, from mortgages to corporate credit.

• The Treasury's larger buybacks signal official concern about market functioning and could cap further spikes.

• Rising yields tighten financial conditions, a headwind for equities and rate-sensitive sectors.
importance:
• The 10-year yield is the global benchmark risk-free rate, anchoring valuations across markets.

• A disorderly bond sell-off can quickly spill into equities, credit and currencies.

• The episode tests the resilience of the world's largest and most systemically important bond market.

title: ECB Hikes to 2.5% as Energy Shock Lifts Eurozone Inflation
content: The European Central Bank raised its key deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on Thursday, its second hike of the year, as an energy-driven jump in eurozone inflation forced policymakers to tighten despite fragile growth. President Christine Lagarde called the unanimous decision 'a no brainer' and warned that the Middle East conflict and Russia's war on Ukraine would keep headline inflation well above the 2% target for an extended period.
summary: The ECB lifted rates to 2.5% to counter an energy-led inflation surge, with Lagarde signalling further tightening ahead.
context:
• Surging oil and gas prices from the Iran war have reignited inflation pressures across the eurozone.

• The ECB had already begun tightening earlier in 2026, reversing an easing bias as energy costs climbed.

• European equities entered the decision under pressure, with a global bond sell-off lifting regional yields.
happened:
• The ECB raised the deposit rate to 2.5% from 2.25% in a unanimous vote, its second increase this year.

• Lagarde described the move as robust across the bank's economic scenarios and flagged upside inflation risks.

• The pan-European STOXX 600 fell 2.2% over the week, its biggest weekly loss since April, while markets priced in further hikes.
implications:
• Additional ECB tightening would raise financing costs for heavily indebted eurozone governments and companies.

• A hawkish ECB could support the euro but weigh on rate-sensitive equity sectors.

• Persistent energy-led inflation leaves the bank caught between price stability and slowing growth.
importance:
• The ECB's pivot back to hiking marks a significant shift for the world's second-largest economic bloc.

• European bond and equity markets are highly sensitive to the pace of further tightening.

• The decision underscores how the oil shock is forcing central banks globally towards a more hawkish stance.

title: Nvidia-Palantir Sovereign-AI Deal Overshadowed by Sell-Off
content: Nvidia and Palantir unveiled a sovereign artificial-intelligence partnership on Thursday, combining Nvidia's Nemotron open models with Palantir's Foundry and AIP software to help governments and companies deploy AI across critical supply chains. Despite the strategic significance, both stocks fell — Nvidia dropping about 2.2% and Palantir around 2% — as surging Treasury yields, oil above $100 and renewed inflation fears pressured high-valuation technology shares.
summary: Nvidia and Palantir announced a sovereign-AI tie-up, but both stocks fell as the macro sell-off hit tech valuations.
context:
• The AI-chip trade has led US equities in 2026, with Nvidia at the centre of market leadership.

• Hyperscaler capital spending is projected to jump from around $800bn in 2026 towards $1.3tn in 2027, underpinning chip demand.

• Richly valued technology names are particularly exposed when interest rates and discount rates rise.
happened:
• The companies said they would integrate Nvidia's Nemotron open-weight models into Palantir's software, with the first deployment inside Nvidia's own supply chain.

• Nvidia shares fell about 2.2% and Palantir dropped roughly 2% on the day.

• The muted reaction came as the 10-year Treasury yield spiked and crude traded above $100 a barrel.
implications:
• Sovereign-AI deals could open a large new market as governments seek control over critical AI infrastructure.

• Continued increases in yields would keep pressure on the elevated valuations underpinning the AI trade.

• Nvidia's direction remains a bellwether for the broader equity market given its index weight.
importance:
• As the market's largest company and AI leader, Nvidia's moves ripple across the major indices.

• The deal signals how AI is expanding from model-building into operational deployment at scale.

• The sell-off despite positive news shows how macro forces are currently overriding company-specific catalysts.
